PathSnap: Distributed Map-Matching & Route Reconstruction

UE24CS352A Machine Learning, PES University (RR Campus) · Technical Report
Team: <names / SRNs> · Section B
Repository: github.com/ankita3454/PathSnap-RouteReconstruction · all numbers below are generated from results/ by report/build_report.py.
Summary. Each GPS fix gets road-arc candidates (radius 50 m, K = 8). A tuned LightGBM classifier scores every candidate, and an HMM/Viterbi decoder turns the scores into a connected route. On the 10 student-test trips (19,160 fixes) the classifier alone reaches 90.04% observation Top-1 accuracy. HMM decoding raises this to 92.51% and lifts route continuity from 94.49% to 98.16%. The reconstructed routes reach a mean length-weighted route F1 of 96.42%.

1. Problem framing

The .route file lists the arcs the vehicle traversed in order, but it does not say which GPS fix belongs to which arc. We therefore (i) derive a reference arc for every fix (Section 2.1), (ii) frame scoring as a binary classification over candidate (fix, arc) pairs: is this candidate the reference arc of this fix?, and (iii) normalise the scores within each fix's candidate set. The result is a probability over candidates, which is exactly what the HMM needs as an emission. Observation-level Top-1 accuracy is the primary selection metric, because it is literally "did we put this fix on the right road". Candidate-row macro-F1 and log loss are reported as required. Log loss matters because the HMM consumes the probabilities.

2. Dataset understanding and EDA

Partitions: EDA statistics use TRAIN and STUDENT_TEST as labelled. Every modelling choice (candidate radius/K, anomaly rule, feature design, hyperparameters, decoder parameters) uses TRAIN only. The evaluator-test partition is not available to us and is never used.

2.1 Raw data and preprocessing

How we preprocessed.

  1. GPS cleaning. We drop non-finite or out-of-range coordinates, sort by timestamp and drop duplicate timestamps. There were 0 missing or invalid values in either partition, and no out-of-order rows, so cleaning changed nothing, but the checks stay in the pipeline for the evaluator trips.
  2. Projection. Trips are spread worldwide (latitude -34.6 to 61.7, longitude -100.4 to 137.2). Degrees are not metres, so every trip is projected with a local equirectangular projection centred on its median fix. Over the extent of one trip the scale error is far below GPS noise, and all later distances are cheap Euclidean metres.
  3. Network cropping. We keep only the arcs with an endpoint inside the trip's GPS bounding box plus 800 m. Networks have up to ~300k arcs, and cropping keeps both candidate search and shortest-path queries fast.
  4. Per-fix reference labels. A monotonic dynamic programme assigns each fix to a position in the route sequence, never going backwards in time, while minimising total fix-to-arc distance (labels.py). This respects the route order, which matters where an arc and its reverse twin overlap or where a route revisits a street. Greedy nearest-arc snapping would get these cases wrong.
  5. Anomalous trips. For train trips 00000033, 00000054, the median distance from a fix to its own reference route is over 50 m (122 m and 140 m), so the GPS and the route do not describe the same path well. Their derived labels are unreliable, and both trips are excluded from training (rule in results/eda/excluded_trips.json). This leaves 78 training trips.
  6. Candidates. Arc geometry is sampled every 10 m into a KD-tree. Each fix takes all arcs within the radius, keeping the K nearest. Radius and K were chosen on TRAIN (table below): 50 m / K = 8 gives a 1.85% candidate miss rate on TRAIN with ~1.0 M candidate rows. Going to 80 m / K = 12 only lowers the miss rate to 0.99% while adding 52 % more rows. On STUDENT_TEST the miss rate is 0.42%.

2.2 Patterns observed

  • Sampling. Nominally 1 Hz: 93.83% of train steps are exactly 1 s, but there are 1216 gaps over 5 s in train (the longest is 153064 s, and one trip spans 1.8 days). Gaps motivate the gap-aware transition model.
  • GPS noise. On TRAIN, the median distance from a fix to its reference arc is 5.7 m, but the tail is heavy: 95th percentile 142 m before excluding the two anomalous trips. Distance alone is not enough near parallel or close roads.
  • Reverse twins. Across all trip networks, 92.31% of arcs have a reverse-direction twin with identical geometry, so for most fixes the two nearest candidates are geometrically tied. Only motion direction (GPS heading) can separate them. This drove the heading features.
  • Network structure. There are no isolated nodes, but the networks are fragmented: the median train network has 20 weakly connected components, and the largest component holds on average 96.90% of nodes. The decoder must therefore tolerate disconnected candidate pairs.
  • Reference routes. 11 of 90 routes are not end-to-end contiguous (consecutive arcs do not share a node), so reference routes have gaps of their own. We avoid overstating label certainty.

2.3 Features and why

We engineered 21 features per (fix, candidate) pair (features.py):

  • Geometry: dist, dist_rank, dist_minus_min, dist_softmax (Gaussian-weighted share of the candidate set). These capture absolute and relative closeness.
  • Direction: head_diff (heading from fixes t-1 to t+1 vs the arc bearing, directed), head_diff_long (t-5 to t+5, robust when slow) and head_diff_undirected. These separate reverse twins and crossing streets.
  • Kinematics: speed, step_len and dt. Heading is unreliable when stationary, and gaps make positions less informative.
  • Temporal context: win_dist_mean and win_dist_max (distance of fixes t-3 to t+3 to the same arc), dist_prev and dist_next. A correct arc stays close over neighbouring fixes, while a crossing street is close for only one fix.
  • Arc and topology: arc_len, proj_frac, proj_overshoot (projection falls beyond the arc end, i.e. the fix is near an intersection), out_deg_to, in_deg_from, has_twin and n_cands.

The most informative features in the tuned model were dist_minus_min (31.33%), head_diff_long (29.32%), proj_overshoot (11.55%), dist_rank (5.63%), arc_len (4.02%) (share of split gain, Fig 13).

3. Model experimentation and comparison

Protocol: 5-fold GroupKFold on the 78 train trips, grouped by trip so that no trip appears in both the fit and validation folds. Each model is then refit on all train trips and evaluated once on the 10 student-test trips. Seed 42 throughout. Per-fold logs are in results/models/cv_folds.csv.

CV macro-F1 and test macro-F1 are computed over candidate rows (threshold 0.5). Top-1 accuracy is per GPS fix, over all 19,160 test fixes; a fix with no correct candidate counts as wrong. Route continuity is the share of consecutive fix pairs whose predicted arcs are the same or directly connected. Inference time is for all candidate rows of the 10 test trips.

Selection. LightGBM and XGBoost are statistically tied on CV macro-F1 (0.9392 vs 0.9396; the difference is far below the fold standard deviation of ~0.010). LightGBM has the best student-test Top-1 (90.05%), joint-best test log loss and a lower training time, and it plugs directly into the decoder through calibrated probabilities. It was selected for Bayesian optimisation. Random Forest is close but 4x slower to train. GaussNB is clearly unsuitable: its log loss of 1.10 shows over-confident, poorly calibrated probabilities.

Where the classifiers fail. Of the 1907 Top-1 errors that untuned LightGBM makes on student-test, 42.00% pick the reverse twin of the correct arc, 78.71% pick an arc that shares a node with the correct arc (intersections), and only 4.25% are fixes whose correct arc was not in the candidate set. Most errors are therefore local and sequential in nature, which is exactly what the HMM is meant to fix.

3.2 Per-model analysis

3.2.1 Model 1: LogReg (Linear / probabilistic)

A.1 Why suitable? A linear baseline on our engineered features: if the right arc is mostly the closest arc with the matching heading, a weighted sum of distance and heading terms should already separate it. It also gives calibrated-ish probabilities that can be plugged straight into the HMM.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: trains in ~2 s, very fast inference, coefficients are interpretable: the largest standardised weights are proj_overshoot (-5.0, fix projects past the arc end), head_diff_long (-1.8), head_diff (-1.0) and dist_minus_min (-1.0). Limitations: it cannot model interactions such as 'heading difference only matters when the vehicle is moving' (speed x head_diff), so it under-uses the heading signal that separates an arc from its reverse twin.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). C = 1.0 (L2), lbfgs, max_iter = 500; inputs are signed-log1p transformed then standardised (fitted inside each training fold).

B.6 Loss / objective. Binary cross-entropy (log loss) + L2 penalty.

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 88.07%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 93.02%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 91.21% and continuity 98.07%. Training time on all train rows 2.2 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 0.02 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.8807, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.9149 (precision of the positive class 0.8730, recall 0.8434), log loss = 0.1269.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.8804, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8799, student-test Top-1 = 0.8807; train log loss = 0.1302 vs CV 0.1320. Verdict: no meaningful over- or under-fitting: train, CV and test scores are close.

3.2.2 Model 2: GaussNB (Linear / probabilistic)

A.1 Why suitable? Included as the simplest probabilistic model: it treats every feature as conditionally independent Gaussians given the label, which tests whether a 'naive' likelihood model is good enough for emissions.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: no tuning, trains in under a second. Limitations: our features are strongly correlated (dist, win_dist_mean, dist_prev, dist_next are all distances to the same arc) and non-Gaussian (heading differences are bimodal: ~0 deg or ~180 deg for twins). The independence assumption double-counts the distance evidence and produces over-confident probabilities, which is visible in its very high log loss.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). var_smoothing = 1e-9 (default); same signed-log1p + scaling as LogReg.

B.6 Loss / objective. No iterative loss: maximum-likelihood estimates of per-class means and variances.

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 80.19%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 90.18%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 89.04% and continuity 97.27%. Training time on all train rows 0.5 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 0.02 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.8019, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.7854 (precision of the positive class 0.5276, recall 0.9147), log loss = 1.0975.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.8019, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8012, student-test Top-1 = 0.8019; train log loss = 1.1270 vs CV 1.1369. Verdict: under-fitting: train, CV and test scores are all low and almost identical, so the model is too simple (strong bias), not over-fitted.

3.2.3 Model 3: KNN (Instance-based)

A.1 Why suitable? An instance-based model: candidates whose feature vectors look like previously seen correct candidates are probably correct. It needs no assumption about the functional form.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: non-parametric, captures local non-linear structure. Limitations: brute-force distance computation scales with the training set, so it was fitted on a 40 000-row random subsample (of ~0.8 M rows per fold); it is the slowest model at inference (several seconds for the test set), and the probabilities are coarse (fractions of 25 neighbours), which hurts log loss.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). k = 25, distance weighting, Euclidean metric on scaled features, 40 000-row training subsample (seed 42).

B.6 Loss / objective. None (lazy learner); predictions are distance-weighted neighbour votes.

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 87.51%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 92.87%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 90.88% and continuity 98.01%. Training time on all train rows 0.0 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 8.08 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.8751, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.9158 (precision of the positive class 0.9076, recall 0.8144), log loss = 0.1464.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.8888, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8746, student-test Top-1 = 0.8751; train log loss = 0.1302 vs CV 0.1515. Verdict: no strong over-fitting on the full training set because it was fitted on a 40k subsample; the train-CV gap is small, but performance is limited by the subsample and coarse neighbour probabilities.

3.2.4 Model 4: RandomForest (Ensemble (bagging))

A.1 Why suitable? Bagged decision trees capture interactions (e.g. heading only matters when speed is high, distance matters relative to the other candidates) without feature scaling, and averaging many trees gives stable probabilities.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: robust, little tuning, near the top on every metric. Limitations: the slowest model to train here (~70 s per fold with 150 trees on 25 % bootstrap samples, 2 cores) and the saved model is large; it was marginally below the boosted models on CV macro-F1 and log loss.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). n_estimators = 150, min_samples_leaf = 10, max_samples = 0.25, max_features = sqrt, seed 42.

B.6 Loss / objective. Gini impurity per split (no global loss); probabilities = mean leaf class frequency.

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 89.06%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 93.68%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 92.00% and continuity 98.16%. Training time on all train rows 93.0 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 0.70 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.8906, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.9328 (precision of the positive class 0.9052, recall 0.8708), log loss = 0.0921.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.9067, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8903, student-test Top-1 = 0.8906; train log loss = 0.0735 vs CV 0.0944. Verdict: no meaningful over- or under-fitting: train, CV and test scores are close.

3.2.5 Model 5: LightGBM (Boosting)

A.1 Why suitable? Gradient-boosted trees fit the residual errors of the previous trees, which suits our tabular, mixed-scale features and the many feature interactions; histogram-based training is fast on ~1 M candidate rows.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: best Top-1 accuracy and joint-best log loss on the student-test trips, fast training with 2 cores, and it provides a training history. Limitations: it can over-fit with many leaves (train Top-1 is higher than CV Top-1, see C.9) and, like every per-candidate classifier, it scores each fix independently, so it cannot enforce route connectivity on its own.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). n_estimators = 400, learning_rate = 0.05, num_leaves = 63, subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8, min_child_samples = 20, reg_lambda = 0.

B.6 Loss / objective. Binary log loss (gradient boosting on the logistic loss).

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 90.05%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 94.23%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 92.41% and continuity 98.18%. Training time on all train rows 20.3 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 1.19 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.9005, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.9365 (precision of the positive class 0.9042, recall 0.8841), log loss = 0.0894.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.9306, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8924, student-test Top-1 = 0.9005; train log loss = 0.0566 vs CV 0.0935. Verdict: mild over-fitting: training Top-1 is 3.8 points above CV Top-1. CV and student-test scores agree, so generalisation is still good; regularisation was one of the levers in the Bayesian search.

3.2.6 Model 6: XGBoost (Boosting)

A.1 Why suitable? A second boosting implementation with depth-wise trees and second-order gradients; included to check whether the boosting result depends on the specific library.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: statistically tied with LightGBM (CV macro-F1 difference well inside one fold standard deviation), fastest of the boosted models at inference. Limitations: same independence-per-fix limitation as all classifiers; slightly lower student-test Top-1 than LightGBM.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). n_estimators = 400, eta = 0.05, max_depth = 7, subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8, tree_method = hist.

B.6 Loss / objective. Binary log loss (logistic objective).

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 89.83%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 94.31%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 92.19% and continuity 98.13%. Training time on all train rows 21.0 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 0.36 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.8983, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.9354 (precision of the positive class 0.9032, recall 0.8814), log loss = 0.0894.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.9271, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8925, student-test Top-1 = 0.8983; train log loss = 0.0602 vs CV 0.0925. Verdict: mild over-fitting: training Top-1 is 3.5 points above CV Top-1. CV and student-test scores agree, so generalisation is still good; regularisation was one of the levers in the Bayesian search.

3.2.7 Model 7: MLP (Neural network)

A.1 Why suitable? A shallow neural network can learn smooth non-linear combinations of the features; with early stopping it is a reasonable neural baseline on tabular data.

A.2 Strengths and limitations. Strengths: competitive accuracy, very fast inference, produces epoch-wise training curves. Limitations: needs feature scaling, is sensitive to the learning rate, and hit the 40-epoch cap in some folds (ConvergenceWarning), so it may be slightly under-trained; it still trailed the tree ensembles.

B.5 Important hyperparameters (initial values). hidden layers (64, 32), ReLU, Adam lr = 1e-3, batch 1024, max_iter = 40, early stopping on a 10 % internal validation split, patience 5.

B.6 Loss / objective. Binary cross-entropy (log loss) with L2 alpha = 1e-4.

C.7 Performance on student-test. Top-1 accuracy 89.41%, route continuity of the raw argmax sequence 94.22%; after HMM decoding with the same decoder settings Top-1 becomes 91.91% and continuity 98.13%. Training time on all train rows 25.2 s, inference on all 19,160 test fixes 0.04 s.

C.8 Observation-level metrics (student-test). Top-1 = 0.8941, candidate-row macro-F1 = 0.9317 (precision of the positive class 0.8971, recall 0.8753), log loss = 0.0977.

C.9 Over/under-fitting. Train (in-sample) Top-1 = 0.9064, 5-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8887, student-test Top-1 = 0.8941; train log loss = 0.0785 vs CV 0.1023. Verdict: no meaningful over- or under-fitting: train, CV and test scores are close.

3.3 Model visualisations

4. Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation (LightGBM)

  1. Hyperparameters searched: num_leaves, learning_rate, n_estimators, min_child_samples, subsample, colsample_bytree, reg_lambda.
  2. Ranges / distributions: num_leaves int 15–127 (log), learning_rate 0.01–0.2 (log), n_estimators 100–500 (step 50), min_child_samples 5–300 (log), subsample 0.5–1.0, colsample_bytree 0.4–1.0, reg_lambda 1e-3–10 (log).
  3. Objective: maximise mean observation-level Top-1 accuracy over 3-fold GroupKFold on TRAIN. Macro-F1 and log loss are logged for every trial (results/bayes/optuna_trials.csv).
  4. Trials: 20 trials of Optuna's TPE sampler (seed 42, 6 random start-up trials), with 17.2 min of total compute. An earlier search with a wider space (num_leaves up to 255, n_estimators up to 800) was stopped after 11 trials because each trial took ~3 min on our hardware. Its log is kept in results/bayes/bayes_aborted_first_search.log, and its best value (0.8950) is in line with the final search.
  5. Best values: num_leaves = 102, learning_rate = 0.09478, n_estimators = 500, min_child_samples = 77, subsample = 0.9448, colsample_bytree = 0.7516, reg_lambda = 1.297 (3-fold CV Top-1 = 0.8953). Our cloud machine restarted after trial 14. The 15 finished trials were re-inserted into the (now SQLite-persistent) Optuna study from the run log by 05a_import_trials_from_log.py, with their parameters, objective values and logged CV metrics unchanged, and the search resumed to 20 trials.
  6. Did tuning help? See the table below. Both models were evaluated with the identical 5-fold protocol and on the same student-test trips.

Honest verdict: tuning did not meaningfully improve the model. The search found a configuration with slightly higher CV Top-1 (5-fold 0.8939 vs 0.8924, +0.15 points), but CV macro-F1 is unchanged (0.9392 vs 0.9392), student-test Top-1 is the same (0.9004 vs 0.9005), and log loss is slightly worse (0.0920 vs 0.0894). The tuned model is also slower (bigger trees, 500 rounds). All 20 trials landed between 0.8775 and 0.8953 (Fig 11), and most were within 0.3 points of each other. Our reading is that the default LightGBM configuration was already near the ceiling these features allow: most remaining errors are reverse-twin and intersection confusions that a per-fix classifier cannot resolve, whatever its hyperparameters. The tuned model is kept as the deployed artifact because it was selected by the pre-declared objective, and its HMM result (Section 5) is within 0.1 points of the untuned model's.

5. HMM and Viterbi route reconstruction

  1. Hidden states. At fix t, the states are its candidates Ct. Each state is an arc together with the projected offset s along that arc, so every state maps one-to-one to an original arc id and the candidate-to-segment correspondence is preserved.
  2. Emissions. log bt(j) = we · log( pj / Σk∈Ct pk + 10-6 ), where p is the tuned LightGBM probability. As a baseline we also ran a classic Gaussian emission (−d²/2σ², σ = 8 m) with no classifier.
  3. Transitions. log a(i→j) = −| droute(i,j) − dgc(t−1,t) | / βt. Here droute is the driving distance from (arci, si) to (arcj, sj): the remainder of arc i, plus the Dijkstra shortest path from its end node to the start node of arc j (cached per source, limit 3 km), plus sj. For the same arc moving forward it is |sj − si|. dgc is the straight-line distance between the two fixes. Routes that wander much more than the GPS moved are penalised.
  4. Missing candidates and gaps. Fixes with an empty candidate set are skipped, and the next transition spans the gap. βt = β·√max(Δt, 1) loosens the transition after time gaps, and the plausible distance grows as vmax·Δt + 50 m (vmax = 60 m/s).
  5. Disconnected segments. If no path exists within the search limit, the path is implausibly long, or the move is backwards on the same arc by more than 8 m, the transition gets a finite penalty (log a = −30) instead of −∞. Viterbi therefore never breaks on fragmented networks: it still prefers connected routes, but it can jump when the network really is disconnected. The decoded per-fix arcs are collapsed into a route, and remaining holes are filled with shortest paths. Holes that cannot be filled are counted as route breaks.
  6. Did HMM help? Yes. The decoder parameters were tuned on out-of-fold TRAIN probabilities (grid below, 20 trips), and the results are reported on STUDENT_TEST:

0000007739110.78880.81850.93990.99260.87221.00000.931801.36
000000918740.90270.92790.90840.96330.93360.99560.963600.38

HMM decoding improved Top-1 accuracy on all 10 student-test trips. Pooled Top-1 rose from 90.04% to 92.51%, continuity rose from 94.49% to 98.16%, and mean route F1 rose from 0.81 (raw argmax arcs) to 0.96. The gains are largest where the classifier flips between a road and its reverse twin or a crossing street (trip 00000056: +3.9 points; trip 00000076: +3.0 points). The HMM helped least on trip 00000007 (+0.4 points), where the classifier was already 94.8% correct and continuity was 99.7%, so there was little to fix. The weakest trip is 00000077 (81.9% after HMM): its errors survive decoding because both readings of the ambiguous stretches are connected routes, so the transition model cannot tell them apart. The Gaussian-emission HMM without a classifier scores 88.71%, which is below even the classifier alone. So the learned emissions, not the decoder by itself, carry most of the accuracy, and the two components are complementary. Every one of the 7 classifiers gains 2.4–8.9 points from the same decoder (table in Section 3.1). Decoding the student-test trips took 0.1–1.5 s per trip. 3 transition steps in 2 trips had no feasible transition and were bridged with the penalty, and 4 route breaks could not be filled by a shortest path.

6. Geographical visualisation (Folium)

Interactive maps for all 10 student-test trips are in results/maps/student_test_*.html, generated by 06_hmm_eval.py using src/pathsnap/viz.py. Layers: road network near the track (grey), raw GPS fixes (blue), reference route (green), predicted HMM route (red), and the classifier-only argmax arcs (amber, toggle). Each map has a legend, a layer control and start/end markers, and is zoomed to the trip extent.

7. API, UI and deployment

Laptop 1 runs uvicorn api.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000. FastAPI loads artifacts/final_model.joblib, model_config.json and hmm_config.json at start-up. POST /predict {"trip_id"} runs cleaning → candidates/features → LightGBM → Viterbi → route reconstruction. Only after that does it read the trip's .route (in evaluate_prediction) to compute accuracy. The reference geometry is never returned. Laptop 2 serves ui/index.html (Leaflet vendored locally). The evaluator enters the API address, sees the trip list from GET /trips, clicks a trip, and the UI draws the GPS and the predicted route and shows Top-1 (HMM and classifier-only), route precision/recall/F1, continuity and timings.

8. Limitations

  • Per-fix labels are derived from the reference route by alignment, so they inherit route gaps (11 non-contiguous routes) and can be ambiguous where twin arcs overlap. Reported accuracies are relative to these derived labels.
  • The two excluded train trips show that some trips have large systematic offsets. A trip like that in the evaluator set would score poorly on Top-1 even with a sensible route.
  • Our continuity metric is strict: when the vehicle crosses a very short arc between two 1 Hz fixes, the two predicted arcs are counted as "not directly connected" even though the reconstructed route fills that arc in.
  • The decoder parameters were tuned on 20 train trips, and a finer grid could add a little more.
